title: Every Nuts And Bolts Fastener Explained In 10 Minutes
fullText: The hex nut. Start with the one everyone already owns a hundred of without noticing. The hex nut is just a cylinder with six flat sides and threading cut into the inside. It works purely on friction. Tighten it down and the threads stretch the bolt slightly and that tension is what locks the whole joint together. The six sides aren't random. [music] A four-sided square nut gives more leverage per turn, but a wrench has to swing a full 90° to get a new grip on it, which is a nightmare in tight machinery. Six sides only need 60° of rotation between grips. It's the [music] exact geometric sweet spot between how much torque a tool can apply and how little room that tool actually needs. And a hex nut is not just a hex nut. Look closely at the top of one and you'll often find tiny stamped lines or numbers. A grade marking that tells you exactly how much stress that specific piece of metal was engineered to survive. The nut holding a garden gate shut and the nut holding a jet engine cowling together can look completely identical. [music] And the only thing separating them is a marking most people never learn to read. The wing nut. The wing nut throws the wrench out entirely. It's a threaded barrel with two wide metal wings sticking out the sides built to be tightened with nothing but your fingers. Those wings just give enough leverage to generate real clamping force by hand. That's why wing nuts show up on anything you're expected to adjust constantly without reaching for a toolbox. Microphone stands, camera rigs, symbol mounts. It trades maximum holding power for maximum convenience on purpose. The nyllock nut. It looks like a standard hex nut with a raised collar sitting on top. And packed inside that collar is a ring of nylon. As the bolt threads pass through, they physically carve into that undersized nylon ring. And the nylon bites back, [music] gripping the threads with enough friction to stop the nut from vibrating loose. It was built to solve a specific problem. machinery shaking itself apart over time, one tiny rotation at a time. A metal lock washer can flatten out and lose its grip completely. But nylon actively clamps the threads instead. The catch is heat. Push a standard nyllock past 250° F and that nylon ring melts, taking the entire locking mechanism with it. That's why you won't find one anywhere near an exhaust manifold or a turbo. For parts that run genuinely hot, engineers swap in an all- metal locking nut instead. One that grips through deformed metal threads rather than nylon because metal doesn't care how hot the engine bay gets. The Acorn nut. It's a hex base with a smooth polished dome capping the top. Functionally, it works exactly like a regular nut, but that dome closes over the exposed end of the bolt instead of leaving it sticking out. People assume it's there purely to stop sharp threads from snagging skin or clothing, and that's part of it. But its real job is hiding the joint entirely, turning [music] an exposed industriallook bolt into something that looks finished and deliberate. The flange nut. It's a hex nut fused to a wide washer-like base, often with ridges cut into the underside. That flange spreads the clamping pressure over a much larger area. So instead of crushing a soft material or getting yanked through an oversized hole, the load gets distributed. It's less a design breakthrough and more a manufacturing shortcut. Forging the nut and the washer as one single piece means a washer can never be left off the line by accident [music] and assembly gets faster across the board. the T-nut, a thin threaded barrel welded to a flat flange. And that flange has three or four sharp prongs jutting out parallel to the barrel. You drive it straight into wood, prongs first, and as a bolt threads in from the opposite side, those prongs get pulled deeper into the timber, [music] locking the whole nut flush and stopping it from spinning in place. It basically lets you install permanent reusable machine threads into a material that was never built to hold them, which is the castle nut. Six deep rectangular slots cut into the top, which is exactly why it looks like the top of a medieval fortress. It's paired with a bolt that has a hole drilled straight through it. Torque the nut down, line up one of those slots with the hole, and push a cotter pin through both. Every other locking nut on this list eventually fails [music] through friction. Nylon melts, threads wear, springs flatten. A castle nut doesn't rely on friction at all. It relies on a physical steel pin blocking rotation completely, which is exactly why it's mandatory in places where a nut backing off isn't an inconvenience. It's a catastrophe. Automotive steering components, aircraft axles. And this is why the nut has six slots instead of just one. The nut has to be torqued to a very precise spec first. And the odds of that exact torque value lining up perfectly with a single slot are basically zero. Six slots means a mechanic can nudge the nut slightly further until any one of them lines up without ever going past the torque the joint calls for. The wood screw, a tapered shaft, a sharp point, and aggressive, widely spaced threads that stop short of the head, leaving a smooth section of shank near the top. That smooth section is the entire trick. It lets the top piece of wood slide freely along the shank while the threads underneath keep [music] pulling so the two pieces get cinched together tightly instead of just being pinned in place. Unlike a bolt going into a pre-made hole, a wood screw carves its own path, compressing the wood fibers around it. And that compression is what holds it in place indefinitely. Machine screw. a blunt cylinder with fine, tight threads running evenly from the tip all the way to the head. And unlike a wood screw, it does not cut its own path. It needs a pre-tapped hole or a matching nut waiting for it. That precision is the entire point. A machine screw is built to be installed and removed thousands of times without wearing the joint down, which is why they're holding together everything from laptop casings to jet engine panels. The selftapping screw threaded all the way to the head with a tip sharp and hard enough to act as its own drill bit. Drive it into thin sheet metal and it does two jobs at once, piercing the material and cutting matching threads into it in the same motion. It works because thin metal is strong enough to snap back tightly around the threads once they're cut, creating a semi-permanent, high friction grip without ever needing a pre-tapped hole. Not all of them actually cut either. Some are built to displace material instead of removing it, pushing plastic or soft metal outward around the threads rather than shaving it away, which leaves a tighter, cleaner grip in materials that would crack if you tried to [music] cut into them. The hexbolt, a thick shaft, partially or fully threaded, topped with a flat six-sided head built to be driven by a wrench or socket. It's the heavy lifter of the entire fastener world. That external head shape is designed specifically to maximize how much torque a tool can transfer into it, which is exactly what's needed to generate the enormous clamping tension holding steel beams and heavy machinery together. The carriage bolt, a smooth rounded dome for a head, and directly underneath it sits a distinct square block of metal. drive it into wood and that square section bites into the timber and locks itself from spinning, which means you only ever need one wrench on the nut on the opposite side. It was born out of a very specific problem in the 1800s. Horsedrawn carriages needed bolts that wouldn't rattle loose over cobblestone roads and could be tightened from a single side in cramped undercarriage spaces. That smooth, rounded head wasn't just for looks, either. It kept exposed hardware from snagging a passing horse, cargo, or clothing. The lag bolt. It's got the heavy hex head of a bolt driven with a wrench, but the tapered point and aggressive threads of a wood screw underneath it needs a pilot hole first and then it bites deep into heavy timber. It exists for the moment a regular wood screw simply can't survive the sheer weight involved, which is why it's usually the only thing standing between an outdoor deck or a retaining wall and gravity. The socket screw, a cylindrical head with a hexagonal hole recessed into the top driven by a tool that sits inside the fastener instead of around it. Because the tool is fully captured inside the head, it can't slip or cam out under heavy torque the way an external wrench sometimes can. And because there's no need for clearance space around the outside of the head, socket screws can be buried deep inside compact machinery, engines, and tight industrial assemblies where a bulky wrench would never fit. The eyebolt. Every fastener so far exists to clamp two things together. [music] The eyebolt does the opposite. It's a threaded shaft topped with a fully closed forged metal loop and it threads into a heavy object to give that object a single dedicated point to be lifted, suspended, or dragged from. It's not holding a joint shut. It's converting the weight of an entire object [music] into one hookup point for a cable, a rope, or a shackle. And if an eyebolt ever fails, the result isn't a loose joint. It's a dropped load. That's why the shape underneath the loop actually matters more than people assume. A shoulder eyebolt has a collar that [music] sits flush against the surface, and that collar is what lets it safely take a load, pulling in at an angle.
